lesson.title: Je veux + Infinitive Gym
lesson.subtitle: Chain the converted verbs into real sentences

hook.title: The Want-Verb Is a Train Engine
hook.content: je veux pulls infinitives the way an engine pulls cars: je veux visiter Paris, je veux organiser une invitation, je veux participer un peu. The second verb never conjugates — it stays in its dictionary form, parked behind the want. This is the same insight as German's modal bracket, wearing French clothes.

pattern.title: Two Verbs, One Sentence, Zero Stress
pattern.content: The rule: only veux bends. The infinitive stays whole, wherever je veux leaves it. That stability is why the -ation engine matters — every converted verb is another car on the train, usable the moment it's built.
pattern.trap_note: The mind wants the second verb to agree with tu: tu veux participes. No — the infinitive never conjugates: tu veux participer.

exercises.explanation: veux bends, visiter doesn't — the infinitive stays in the dictionary.

exercises.idea: I want to get involved a little
cues: The everyday register: participer (not the formal-sounding English)
the tag rides at the end: un peu
exercises.meaning: I want to get involved a little
exercises.explanation: Formal English, everyday French — register travels in reverse across the Channel.

exercises.idea: you want to organize the invitation
exercises.meaning: You want to organize the invitation
exercises.explanation: Two conversions in one sentence: the engine (-ation) and the elision (l').

diagnosis.slip: the infinitive picked up an ending
diagnosis.cue: Only veux conjugates. organiser stays whole after tu veux — the second verb is parked, not driven.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentences express the natural thought of 'Je veux participer un peu'?
exercises.meaning: I want to get involved / participate a little
renderings: I want to get involved a little
I want to take part a bit
traps: I don't want to participate at all
exercises.target_answer: I want to get involved a little
exercises.explanation: participer is everyday French for 'getting involved' or 'taking part' — register travels in reverse across the Channel.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: I want to confirm the reservation
cues: Engine car 2: la réservation — with its é
exercises.explanation: Noun and verb from the same Latin root, one sentence apart.
exercises.affirmation: You kept confirmer bare and gave réservation its é — both conversions held.

summary.outcome: Chain converted infinitives after je veux / tu veux with the second verb parked and un-conjugated.

use_example.english: Do you want to organize the invitation?

summary.takeaway: Only the want-verb bends. The infinitive is parked freight — and every -ation noun is a new car.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([303] The -ir & -re Verb Bridges): see how Je veux + Infinitive Gym leads directly into The -ir & -re Verb Bridges.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "You want to visit Paris" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Tu veux visiter Paris" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Je veux + Infinitive Gym.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

visiter.etymology_derivation: visitation → visiter. The rare English noun unlocks the everyday verb: don't decide too quickly that you can't say it.

participer.context_translation: I want to get involved a little.
participer.etymology_derivation: participation → participer. 'To get involved' sounds formal in English but everyday in French — register travels in reverse.

organiser.etymology_derivation: organisation → organiser. One S in French, even where English writes Z.

confirmer.etymology_derivation: confirmation → confirmer. Strip -ation, bolt on -er (pronounced /e/), and the noun becomes the verb.

un_peu.etymology_derivation: Latin paucus 'a small amount' gave English 'paucity' and French peu — one root, two registers.

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.
